nameStory: The long-tailed weasel gets its name from its most obvious feature - that exceptionally long, bushy tail that makes up about half its total body length! While other weasels have relatively short tails, this species sports a magnificent plume that's impossible to miss. It's also called the 'bridled weasel' because of the distinctive white facial markings that look like a horse's bridle around its dark eyes and nose.
description: The long-tailed weasel is a sleek, snake-like predator with an incredibly elongated body and surprisingly short legs. Think of a furry tube with a disproportionately long, black-tipped tail that seems almost too big for its body. These agile hunters typically measure about the length of a ruler including their tail, with males being noticeably larger than females. Their body shape is perfectly designed for pursuing prey into tight spaces like burrows and rock crevices.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Extremely long, slender body with short legs and an elongated neck - imagine a furry snake with legs. The tail makes up nearly half the total body length and is distinctly bushy compared to the lean body.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Rich brown coat in summer that turns pure white in winter, except for the jet-black tail tip that remains dark year-round. The fur feels dense and soft, with white markings around the chin and sometimes on the chest.

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Small, round paw prints about the size of a quarter, often in a bounding pattern with paired front and back prints. In snow, you'll see drag marks from their low-slung body between footprints.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves with a distinctive arching, bounding gait like a tiny horse galloping. Often stands upright on hind legs to survey surroundings, and can climb trees surprisingly well for such a ground-oriented predator.

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Twisted, rope-like scat about the thickness of a pencil, often deposited on logs or rocks. May find caches of prey items in abandoned burrows or hollow logs, with a distinctive musky scent marking the area.

habitat: Long-tailed weasels prefer edge habitats where forests meet open areas, particularly loving old stone walls, fencerows, and brushy drainage ditches. They're commonly found in mixed woodlands with rocky outcrops and fallen logs that provide hunting opportunities and den sites. You'll often spot them near old barns, woodpiles, and overgrown fields where rodent prey is abundant.

seasonality.spring: Active and highly visible during breeding season, with males traveling extensively and often seen crossing roads or paths in broad daylight. This is when you're most likely to observe their characteristic bounding gait.
seasonality.summer: Wearing rich brown coats, they're busy hunting and raising young. Look for them early morning and evening around rock walls and brush piles where chipmunks and voles are active.
seasonality.fall: Coat begins changing to white starting in October, creating a patchy brown-and-white appearance. Increased activity as they cache food and establish winter territories.
seasonality.winter: Brilliant white except for black tail tip and nose, making them highly visible against snow. Follow their distinctive tracks and body drag marks to locate active areas around rodent burrows.

funFact: A long-tailed weasel can kill and drag prey twice its own body weight, then perform an incredible feat of strength by hauling a full-grown rabbit up a tree to cache it in a hollow - imagine a house cat dragging a medium-sized dog up into the branches!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with the short-tailed weasel (stoat), but remember 'long tail, long weasel' - if the tail is more than 6 inches long with that prominent black tip, you're looking at a long-tailed weasel. The short-tailed species has a much stubbier tail that's less than half the length.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'weasel' having negative connotations, these are actually beneficial predators that help control rodent populations around farms and homes. The term 'weasel word' comes from the misconception that weasels suck eggs, when they actually bite them and lap up the contents - much more efficient than sucking!
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the American mink in the same genus, the long-tailed weasel is much more terrestrial and has a leaner build. Minks are semi-aquatic with webbed feet, darker fur year-round, and prefer waterside habitats, while long-tailed weasels stick to dry land and undergo dramatic seasonal color changes. The weasel's tail is also proportionally much longer and more prominent than a mink's.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American mink are much more aquatic than their closest relative, the long-tailed weasel, and have denser, more water-resistant fur.
